lessonTitle: Venous Drainage and Lymphatics of the Limbs

blocks.text: A 48-year-old shop assistant who stands all day notices twisted, bulging veins along the inside of her calf and an aching heaviness by evening. Her legs have the same blood supply as everyone else's, so the explanation lies in how blood returns uphill and in the small flaps of tissue that normally stop it falling back.

blocks.markdown: Blood returns from the limb in two systems of veins: **superficial veins** in the subcutaneous tissue, and **deep veins** within the muscle compartments, which usually accompany arteries. They are linked by **perforating veins** that pass through the deep fascia. **Lymphatic vessels** drain tissue fluid and run to groups of lymph nodes. In both systems, anatomy explains common clinical problems such as venepuncture, varicose veins and the spread of infection.

blocks.title: Superficial, deep and perforating veins
blocks.text: Superficial veins lie in the subcutaneous fat, outside the deep fascia. Deep veins lie beneath the deep fascia, within or between muscles, and accompany the main arteries as paired venae comitantes (for small arteries) or as a single named vein (for large ones, such as the femoral vein). Perforating veins pierce the deep fascia and carry blood from the superficial to the deep system. Valves in the perforating veins permit flow only in that direction.

rows: Cephalic (lateral side, runs in the deltopectoral groove and drains into the axillary vein); basilic (medial side, joins the brachial veins to form the axillary vein); median cubital vein (links the cephalic and basilic veins in the cubital fossa)
Paired venae comitantes of the radial, ulnar and brachial arteries; axillary vein

Great saphenous (from the medial end of the dorsal venous arch, passes in front of the medial malleolus, up the medial leg and thigh, and drains into the femoral vein at the saphenofemoral junction); small saphenous (from the lateral end, behind the lateral malleolus, up the back of the calf, and drains into the popliteal vein)
Venae comitantes of the tibial and fibular arteries; popliteal vein; femoral vein
blocks.caption: Superficial and deep veins of the limbs.

blocks.markdown: In the upper limb, the **median cubital vein** crosses the cubital fossa and is the commonest site for taking blood (venepuncture) because it is large, superficial and fixed in place; the brachial artery and median nerve lie deeper, beneath the bicipital aponeurosis. In the lower limb the **great saphenous vein** is the longest vein in the body. It runs in front of the medial malleolus (a site for emergency cut-down access) and ends in the femoral vein about 3 to 4 cm below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, where it passes through the saphenous opening in the deep fascia of the thigh.

blocks.title: Direction of venous flow
blocks.prompt: Explain how blood flows from a skin vein on the medial calf to the heart, and why the valves in the perforating veins matter.

steps.text: Blood from the skin collects in the great saphenous vein.
During walking the calf muscles contract and squeeze the deep veins (the calf muscle pump), propelling blood towards the heart.

Perforating veins carry blood from the superficial to the deep veins, and their valves ensure that flow goes only in this direction, so the high pressure generated in the deep veins is not transmitted to the superficial veins.

blocks.answer: Blood flows from superficial veins through perforators into deep veins, which are pumped by the calf muscles; the valves prevent backflow into the superficial system.

blocks.title: Varicose veins
blocks.text: Varicose veins are dilated, tortuous superficial veins, most often in the territory of the great saphenous vein. When valves at the saphenofemoral junction, in the saphenous vein or in perforating veins become incompetent, blood leaks backwards (reflux) and pressure in the superficial veins rises, especially during standing or walking. Over time the veins stretch, become dilated and tortuous, and their valve cusps no longer meet, which worsens the problem. Common associations include prolonged standing, pregnancy, obesity and family history.

blocks.markdown: **Lymphatic drainage.** Lymph from the **upper limb** drains along superficial vessels (following the cephalic and basilic veins) and deep vessels to the **axillary lymph nodes**; a few vessels first pass through cubital (supratrochlear) nodes near the elbow. The axillary nodes are arranged in groups (lateral, pectoral or anterior, subscapular or posterior, central and apical); most of the upper limb drains to the **lateral group**. The axillary nodes also drain the breast and the chest wall, which explains why breast cancer commonly spreads there. In the **lower limb**, the superficial lymphatics of most of the leg follow the great saphenous vein to the **superficial inguinal nodes**; those of the lateral foot and back of the calf follow the small saphenous vein to the **popliteal nodes**. The deep vessels also drain to the popliteal nodes. Both groups drain to the **deep inguinal nodes**, then to the external iliac nodes.

rows: Axillary nodes (mainly the lateral group); cubital nodes for the medial forearm and hand
Apical axillary nodes, then the subclavian lymph trunk
Superficial tissues of the leg and thigh, gluteal region, lower anterior abdominal wall and perineum
Deep inguinal nodes, then the external iliac nodes
Lateral foot and posterior calf (small saphenous territory); deep structures of the leg
blocks.caption: Main lymph node groups draining the limbs.

blocks.title: Infection of the foot
blocks.prompt: A patient has an infected cut on the medial side of the big toe, and tender swelling in the groin. Which nodes are involved, and why?

steps.text: The medial side of the foot drains by superficial lymph vessels that follow the great saphenous vein.
These vessels end in the superficial inguinal nodes in the groin.
Infected lymph reaching the nodes causes lymphadenitis, which is tender enlargement.

blocks.answer: Superficial inguinal nodes, because the medial foot drains along the great saphenous vein to them.

items: Upper limb: cephalic and basilic veins; median cubital vein for venepuncture.
Lower limb: great saphenous vein (medial; to the femoral vein) and small saphenous vein (lateral and posterior; to the popliteal vein).
Perforating veins connect superficial to deep veins and have valves.
Lymph from the upper limb goes to the axillary nodes; from the lower limb to the inguinal (and popliteal) nodes.

blocks.title: Direction of flow
blocks.text: The valves of the limb veins keep blood moving toward the heart and from superficial to deep. Failure of valves does not simply cause swelling; it reverses the direction of flow and creates the dilated tortuous veins seen in varicosities.

points: Limb veins form superficial and deep systems joined by perforating veins; the cephalic and basilic veins in the arm, and the great and small saphenous veins in the leg, are the main superficial veins.
Varicose veins arise when valves at the saphenofemoral junction or in perforators fail, causing reflux and high pressure in the superficial veins.
Lymph from the upper limb drains to the axillary nodes, and lymph from the lower limb to the inguinal nodes, with the popliteal nodes draining the small saphenous territory.

questions.stem: Which vein is the most common site for venepuncture in the cubital fossa?

distractorRationale.b: The brachial veins are deep and accompany the brachial artery.
distractorRationale.c: The axillary vein is deep in the axilla.
distractorRationale.d: The great saphenous vein is in the lower limb.

questions.explanation: The median cubital vein is large, superficial and fixed, and links the cephalic and basilic veins. The deeper brachial artery and median nerve are protected beneath the bicipital aponeurosis.

questions.stem: Where does the great saphenous vein pass at the ankle?

options.text: In front of the medial malleolus
In front of the lateral malleolus

questions.correctOptionText: In front of the medial malleolus

distractorRationale.b: The small saphenous vein passes behind the lateral malleolus.
distractorRationale.c: The posterior tibial vessels pass behind the medial malleolus.
distractorRationale.d: No named superficial vein of note passes here.

questions.explanation: The great saphenous vein begins at the medial end of the dorsal venous arch and passes in front of the medial malleolus. It ascends on the medial side of the leg and thigh to join the femoral vein.

questions.stem: Into which vein does the small saphenous vein drain?

distractorRationale.b: The great saphenous vein drains into the femoral vein.
distractorRationale.c: The external iliac vein is higher.
distractorRationale.d: The small saphenous vein usually drains into the popliteal vein, not the great saphenous.

questions.explanation: The small saphenous vein runs behind the lateral malleolus and up the back of the calf to end in the popliteal vein behind the knee. The great saphenous vein, by contrast, ends in the femoral vein.

questions.stem: In which direction do the valves of perforating veins permit blood to flow?

options.text: From superficial veins to deep veins
From deep veins to superficial veins

questions.correctOptionText: From superficial veins to deep veins

distractorRationale.b: This is the abnormal direction seen with incompetent valves.
distractorRationale.c: Valves direct flow towards the heart.

questions.explanation: Perforating veins carry blood from the superficial to the deep system, where the muscle pump drives it upward. Their valves prevent the high pressure of the deep veins from being transmitted to the superficial veins.

questions.stem: Which mechanism best explains varicose veins in the territory of the great saphenous vein?

options.text: Incompetent valves allow blood to flow backwards, raising pressure in the superficial veins
Narrowing of the femoral artery reduces blood supply
Blockage of the lymphatics by tumour
Excess contraction of the calf muscles

questions.correctOptionText: Incompetent valves allow blood to flow backwards, raising pressure in the superficial veins

distractorRationale.b: Arterial narrowing causes ischaemia, not varicosities.
distractorRationale.d: Calf muscle contraction normally pumps blood upward.

questions.explanation: When valves fail, blood refluxes into the superficial veins under pressure. The veins dilate and become tortuous, which in turn stretches the valve rings further.

questions.stem: A patient has an infected cut on the medial side of the big toe and tender enlarged nodes in the groin. Which nodes are most likely involved?

distractorRationale.b: The axillary nodes drain the upper limb.
distractorRationale.c: Popliteal nodes drain the lateral foot and posterior calf, and the nodes in the groin are not popliteal.
distractorRationale.d: The cubital nodes drain the medial forearm and hand.

questions.explanation: The medial foot drains along the great saphenous vein to the superficial inguinal nodes. Tender swelling there suggests lymphadenitis from infection in this territory.

questions.stem: Which group of lymph nodes receives most lymph from the upper limb?

distractorRationale.b: Inguinal nodes drain the lower limb.
distractorRationale.c: Popliteal nodes drain part of the lower limb.
distractorRationale.d: Internal iliac nodes drain pelvic structures.

questions.explanation: Most of the lymph from the upper limb drains to the lateral group of axillary nodes, either directly or after passing the cubital nodes. The axillary nodes also drain the breast.

questions.stem: True or false: the cephalic vein drains into the axillary vein.

distractorRationale.b: The cephalic vein runs in the deltopectoral groove and drains into the axillary vein.

questions.explanation: The cephalic vein runs up the lateral side of the arm in the deltopectoral groove and pierces the clavipectoral fascia to join the axillary vein. The basilic vein, in contrast, joins the brachial veins to form the axillary vein.

questions.stem: Distinguish superficial from deep veins of the limbs, explain the role of perforating veins, and explain how valve failure leads to varicose veins.
markingGuide: Superficial veins lie in subcutaneous tissue (cephalic, basilic, great and small saphenous); deep veins lie beneath the deep fascia and accompany arteries.
Perforating veins pass through the deep fascia and carry blood from superficial to deep veins.
Valves ensure one-way flow towards the heart and from superficial to deep.
Failed valves (for example at the saphenofemoral junction or in perforators) allow reflux and raise pressure in superficial veins.
questions.explanation: The calf muscle pump drives blood through the deep veins, and valves prevent reflux. If valves are incompetent, high pressure from the deep system or from reflux dilates the superficial veins.

questions.stem: Describe the lymph node groups that drain the upper and lower limbs.
markingGuide: Upper limb: axillary nodes, mainly the lateral group; some lymph passes through cubital nodes.
Axillary groups: lateral, pectoral, subscapular, central and apical.
Lower limb superficial: superficial inguinal nodes along the great saphenous vein.
Lateral foot and back of calf: popliteal nodes.
Deep inguinal nodes then external iliac nodes.
questions.explanation: Each limb drains to a first-station group along the main superficial veins. Knowing the territory of each group helps you trace infection or cancer spread.
